newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss reject calls to freeze Mobutu accounts.
newsitem.headline: Swiss reject calls to freeze Mobutu accounts.

text.p: The Swiss government on Thursday rejected demands by Zairean rebels and Swiss politicians that it freeze billions of dollars Zaire's embattled ruler Mobutu Sese Seko may have deposited in Switzerland.
The Federal Council, or cabinet, said it had decided not to act because Mobutu was still head of state and there was no request from Zairean authorities for legal aid.
"The council concluded that freezing accounts would not be appropriate," the cabinet said in a statement after meeting late on Wednesday.
"The Federal Council is aware that the situation in Zaire is politically and militarily very delicate and is following developments with the corresponding attentiveness," it added.
"The Federal Council also notes that no other state has taken measures in this direction," the statement said.

Zairean rebels have urged Swiss authorities to freeze any wealth Mobuto may have on deposit in Switzerland, a call echoed byu some Swiss members of parliament and activist group Action on Swiss-Third World Finances.
"The Federal Council has no accurate information about the extent of these assets in Switzerland," the statement said.
Mobutu's holdings in Switzerland have been estimated by Swiss media at around $4 billion, although the Swiss Bankers Association say there is no evidence for this.
The Federal Banking Commission has said it has made an informal inquiry among leading Swiss banks but has heard nothing about big Mobutu accounts.
Bankers have said their institutes had learned a lesson from 1980s scandals about dictators' money and would be reluctant to keep politically controversial accounts.
Swiss banks came under heavy criticism in the 1980s for holding accounts from such toppled strongmen as Ferdinand Marcos of the Philippines and Haiti's Jean-Claude "Baby Doc" Duvalier.

Federal Banking Commission director Daniel Zuberbuehler said Mobutu's case had to be treated differently than that of Marcos, whose accounts were frozen by an emergency decree from Berne in 1986 after his ouster.
"Marcos was already toppled. With Mobutu, the throne is shaky but he is still sitting in it," Zuberbuehler told Swiss television.

Berne politicians have said the 1986 emergncy decree was a rare temporary measure to give the new Philippines government time to prepare formal charges against Marcos and request international legal help.
Zaire's AFDL rebel allaince said last month it was seeking legal assistance from Berne in the case, although the Foreign Ministry said it was not aware of any petition.
Berne argues the rebels have no basis to act because only governments can ask for international legal assistance from authorities in another country.
